text: Every magazine you've ever read is named after an Arabic word... and it has nothing to do with reading.
Makhaazin. Storehouses: the places where you keep the grain, the oil, the goods.
Its root means to store away, to keep safe. Put ma in front, and you get the place where you keep things.
Italian made it magazzino. French made it magasin, and in France a magasin is still a shop. In the 1580s, English took it as magazine: a storehouse.
So how does a storehouse end up on a news stand? In 1731, a London monthly called itself The Gentleman's Magazine: a storehouse of articles. The name stuck.
Your turn. The same root is in surah Yusuf. Yusuf tells the king: put me in charge of the khazaa-in of the land. The armies, the roads, or the storehouses?
قالَ اجْعَلْنِي عَلى خَزائِنِ الْأَرْضِ إِنِّي حَفِيظٌ عَلِيمٌ
STOREHOUSES! Put me over the storehouses of the land: I'm a knowing guardian. And he saved the grain for seven hard years.
So which English word should we trace back next? Comment it!
